T-Systems (T Cloud Public).summary_note:
T Cloud Public (rebranded from Open Telekom Cloud in January 2026) is Deutsche Telekom/T-Systems' sovereign public cloud platform, operating exclusively in EU data centres (Biere and Magdeburg, Germany; Aalsmeer and Almere, Netherlands). Its sovereignty profile is strong on legal jurisdiction, operational independence, security certifications, and environmental credentials — but carries a well-documented and structurally unresolved dependency on Huawei (China) for its core cloud operating system (Huawei FusionSphere/Huawei OpenStack Distribution) and partially for server hardware. This creates the central sovereignty tension: T-Systems operates the platform independently with no Huawei system access enforced contractually and procedurally, yet cannot fully audit or sustain the underlying cloud OS without Huawei's continued software support.

Key corrections applied after cross-provider consistency review: (1) SOV-1 Q2 receives P (not Y) — no formal golden share or change-of-control covenant exists, only state ownership-based deterrence; consistent with how other providers are scored. (2) SOV-2 Q5 receives N (not P) — Huawei FusionSphere IP is Chinese-origin, a genuine distinction from EU-native clouds (Hetzner, STACKIT) that build on open-source Linux/KVM. (3) SOV-3 Q5 receives P (not Y) — the original Y incorrectly attributed the Industrial AI Cloud to T Cloud Public; corrected to P (not N) because EU inference governance exists and is consistent with how other providers hosting non-EU AI model software are assessed. (4) SOV-4 Q1 remains Y — T Cloud Public is OpenStack Powered, same basis as other EU providers; PaaS lock-in exists but does not override IaaS portability at this question's scope. (5) SOV-4 Q6 receives N (not P) — Huawei as cloud OS vendor is an additional critical non-EU software dependency beyond the standard Intel/NVIDIA hardware that all EU providers share (P-level); the OS-layer dependency is qualitatively more fundamental. (6) SOV-5 Q4 receives N (not P) — FusionSphere constitutes significant reliance on a non-EU proprietary technology at the platform level, distinct from hardware. (7) SOV-6 Q1 remains Y — OpenStack Powered certification at the IaaS layer is the applicable standard, consistent with other EU providers. (8) SOV-7 Q1 note corrected: EU Cloud Code of Conduct was Level 2, not Level 3. (9) T-Systems North America Inc. and Deutsche Telekom's ownership of T-Mobile US create a potential US nexus noted in SOV-2 Q2.

On the positive side, T Cloud Public holds the most comprehensive EU certification portfolio of any EU public cloud provider (BSI C5 Type 2, ISO 27001/17/18/27701, SOC 1/2/3 Type II, TISAX Level 3), was approved for German federal procurement through GovTech Deutschland (May 2026), offers genuine BYOK+HYOK encryption, operates 100% renewable electricity, and achieves a best-in-class PUE of 1.28 (Biere). The operational model — T-Systems-only EU staff, zero Huawei production access, Huawei video-conference consultation only — is a genuine and enforced design principle. Deutsche Telekom's dual-vendor hardware strategy and the separately launched Industrial AI Cloud (NVIDIA DGX-based, Huawei-free) represent the trajectory toward a fully sovereign technology stack, but as of mid-2026, the Huawei FusionSphere cloud OS dependency remains the defining unresolved sovereignty gap for T Cloud Public.
